entry.title: I just launched TL;Dev, a curated collection of notes for developers and indie builders.
entry.summary: Hey everyone, Like many of you, I spend a lot of time on Reddit, X, and YouTube looking for interesting case studies and strategies. The problem is, there's too much content and not enough time. I'd save dozens of links intending to read them later, but that "later" never came. So, I built a solution for myself called TL;Dev. It's a simple, no-BS website where I personally curate and summarize the most valuable content into short, easy-to-read notes. The goal is to help developers and indie builders grasp the core ideas in minutes, not hours. My site is covering everything from successful launches to costly failures. It's 100% free, no paywall, no annoying pop-ups. Just content. For those interested, it’s built with Astro and deployed on Cloudflare. It's ridiculously fast. I'm posting here because I think it could be genuinely useful for this community, and I'd love to get your feedback on the site, the content, or any ideas you might have. You can check it out here: https://tldev.co Thanks for reading!!

entry.title: What We Mean When We Say "Native TypeScript Support"
entry.summary:
If you’re using Node.js v23.6 or later, you probably know that you can now run TypeScript files directly, without using ts-node, Babel, or a similar build step. Whereas earlier versions of node would have required flags like --experimental-strip-types, as of v23.6, the following will just work: node my-awesome-typescript-code.ts
At first glance, this appears to be Node.js gaining "native TypeScript support", and in a way, it has. However, all that means is that it can convert TypeScript into JavaScript on its own. It does not mean Node understands or enforces TypeScript types at runtime. When you run a .ts file in Node 23.6+, here’s what happens: Node removes TypeScript-specific syntax like : string, : number, interface, etc. from your source code by overwriting it with spaces.
